reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: Hereditary nephrogenic diabetes insipidus reflects collecting-duct resistance to vasopressin, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine despite adequate or high antidiuretic hormone
The majority of inherited cases are X-linked from AVPR2 mutations affecting the V2 receptor, so affected infants are typically boys
A minority are autosomal (recessive or dominant) from AQP2 water-channel mutations and affect both sexes
Infants present with polyuria, poor feeding, unexplained fevers, irritability, vomiting and hypernatraemic dehydration
The biochemical picture is dilute urine with a rising serum sodium and osmolality when free water is not replaced
A water-deprivation test with a vasopressin analogue distinguishes the nephrogenic form (no urinary concentration after the analogue) from central diabetes insipidus

Management centres on unrestricted access to water, a low-solute diet, and measures such as thiazide diuretics with dietary sodium restriction to reduce urine volume rather than vasopressin replacement
reference.pathophysiology: In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus the principal cells of the collecting duct fail to respond to vasopressin. X-linked disease results from loss-of-function mutations in AVPR2, the gene for the V2 vasopressin receptor, so hormone binding cannot trigger the intracellular signalling that normally inserts water channels into the apical membrane. Autosomal forms result from mutations in AQP2, the aquaporin-2 water channel itself, impairing its trafficking or function. Either defect prevents water reabsorption, producing large volumes of inappropriately dilute urine, a tendency to hypernatraemia and dehydration, and compensatory polydipsia.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from lithium or hypercalcaemia
Osmotic diuresis from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
Post-obstructive or tubulointerstitial disease causing a concentrating defect
additionalInvestigations: Paired serum and urine osmolality with serum sodium
Water-deprivation test followed by a vasopressin analogue to localise the defect
Copeptin or vasopressin measurement where available to support classification
Exclusion of hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia and drug (lithium) causes
Renal ultrasound for hydronephrosis or a distended bladder from chronic high urine output
Genetic testing of AVPR2 and AQP2 with carrier assessment in relatives
redFlags: Hypernatraemic dehydration in an infant with lethargy or seizures
Recurrent unexplained fevers and failure to thrive in a young child
Obstructive uropathy or hydronephrosis from chronic high-volume output
Rapid correction of chronic hypernatraemia risking cerebral oedema
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, reliable access to water and volume-reducing measures, growth and development are usually preserved, but repeated episodes of severe hypernatraemic dehydration in infancy can cause lasting neurological injury.
pitfalls: Mistaking the disorder for central diabetes insipidus and expecting a response to vasopressin replacement
Restricting fluids in an infant who depends on free access to water
Correcting chronic hypernatraemia too quickly and precipitating cerebral oedema
Overlooking a treatable acquired cause such as lithium or hypercalcaemia before labelling disease hereditary
management: Guarantee unrestricted access to water, feeding infants frequently, as they cannot signal thirst and are prone to hypernatraemic dehydration
Reduce urine volume with a low-solute (low-sodium, low-protein) diet and a thiazide diuretic
Add amiloride or an NSAID such as indometacin to augment the reduction in polyuria
Monitor serum sodium and osmolality and follow growth and neurodevelopment closely through childhood
Treat hypernatraemic episodes with cautious rehydration to avoid rapid osmotic shifts
Confirm the diagnosis with AVPR2 and AQP2 genetic testing and provide counselling and carrier assessment for relatives given the X-linked and rarer autosomal inheritance
